pages.text: Two days before Eid, Grandma Noura slipped on the kitchen floor and hurt her wrist. The doctor said she had to rest it for three weeks, which meant no cooking at all. Every year, the whole family gathered at her house for her famous chicken kabsa, and nobody had ever made it except her. "Who will cook it this time?" asked Reem, who was thirteen and secretly loved being in the kitchen.

Grandma smiled and pointed to an old notebook on the shelf. "Everything you need is in there," she said. But when Reem opened it, her heart sank. Someone had spilled tea on the kabsa page years ago, and the amounts of the spices had become brown smudges that nobody could read.

Her younger brother, Saud, offered to help, although he had never cooked anything more difficult than an omelette. "How hard can it be?" he said, chopping onions with tears running down his face. He turned the heat up high to save time, and within minutes the kitchen was full of smoke. The onions were black, and they had to start again from the beginning.

By evening, they had finished their first attempt, and they were feeling rather proud of themselves. Then their father tasted it and tried very hard to keep a straight face. "It's... interesting," he said politely, reaching for a glass of water. Reem took a spoonful and almost choked, because they had added far too much salt and almost no spices at all.

That night, Reem couldn't sleep, so she sat in the quiet kitchen and closed her eyes. She tried to remember standing next to Grandma when she was small, watching the big pot bubble. Slowly, the smells came back to her: warm cinnamon, sweet cardamom, and something sharp and smoky that she couldn't name. Suddenly she remembered Grandma breaking small dark balls into the pot and letting her smell them first.

In the morning, she searched the cupboards until she found a jar of dried black limes, called loomi. "That's it!" she shouted, so loudly that Saud dropped his breakfast. This time, they cooked the onions slowly until they were golden, and they tasted the sauce again and again before adding anything else. Little by little, they got the hang of it, and the kitchen began to smell exactly like Eid.

On the first day of Eid, aunts, uncles and cousins filled the house, and Reem felt butterflies in her stomach. She and Saud carried the huge tray of rice and chicken into the majlis and placed it in front of Grandma. Everyone went quiet as Grandma took her first bite with her good hand. She chewed slowly, said nothing for a long moment, and then her eyes filled with tears.

"This tastes just like my mother's kabsa," she said softly, and the whole room cheered. Later, Reem admitted that she had never been able to read the smudged page. Grandma laughed and said, "Neither could I, habibti. I stopped using that book forty years ago, because the real recipe was always in my nose and my heart." Then she placed the old notebook in Reem's hands and told her it was hers to keep, and to fill with her own recipes one day.

options: You should always measure ingredients carefully.

Old recipe books are not useful for young cooks.

pages.text: Faisal had always thought his grandfather's old cassette player was just a piece of junk. Then one evening in Jeddah, while he was helping to clean the storeroom, he found a dusty box of tapes labelled in faded handwriting. One of them said "The Sea Songs, 1975." When Faisal asked what it meant, his grandfather went quiet for a long moment.

"Before oil changed everything, my father was a pearl diver," Grandpa Saleh explained. "The men used to sing on the boats to keep their rhythm while they pulled the heavy ropes. Each boat had a singer called the nahham, and his voice could be heard across the water." He smiled sadly. "I recorded my father singing when he was old, but I've forgotten most of the words, and I haven't listened to that tape for years."

Faisal's school was planning a Heritage Day, and every class had to present something from the past. Faisal had an idea: what if his class could bring the sea songs back to life? His friends Omar and Yousef were excited, but there was a problem. When they played the tape, it twisted and snapped after only twenty seconds.

Faisal refused to give up. He carefully repaired the broken tape, the way he had seen in an online video, and copied the recording onto his laptop. The sound was crackly, and some words were impossible to understand. Still, he could hear a deep, powerful voice, waves in the background, and dozens of men clapping in perfect time.

For two weeks, the boys practised every afternoon. Omar, who was good at drumming, played the rhythm on a small drum borrowed from the school, while the others clapped and answered the singer's lines. Yousef searched the library and discovered an old book about pearl diving that contained some of the missing words. Gradually, the song began to sound less like a lesson and more like a real conversation between a leader and his crew.

On the morning of Heritage Day, Faisal felt as if his stomach was full of butterflies. The hall was packed with families, and his grandfather was sitting in the front row, leaning on his walking stick. Faisal had planned to sing the leader's part himself, but suddenly his voice felt tiny. "If I make a mistake in front of Grandpa," he whispered to Omar, "I'll never forgive myself."

Omar began the drumbeat, and the class started clapping slowly, like oars hitting the water. Faisal took a deep breath and sang the first line, his voice shaking at first but growing stronger. Then, near the end, he reached a line that nobody had been able to find, and he froze. In the silence, a deep, rough voice rose from the front row and finished the line perfectly.

Grandpa Saleh was on his feet, singing words he hadn't sung for fifty years. The boys answered him, the audience began to clap along, and for a moment the whole hall seemed to rock like a boat on the waves. Afterwards, with tears in his eyes, Grandpa told Faisal that hearing the song had brought the missing words back to him. "You didn't just fix a tape," he said, hugging his grandson. "You gave me back my father's voice."

pages.text: Lina was thirteen, and she had read every detective novel in her school library at least twice. She always carried a small blue notebook, just in case a real mystery ever came her way. That Friday, the whole family had gathered at her grandmother's house in Taif. Before the noon prayer, Grandmother took off her gold ring, placed it on the bathroom windowsill and washed for prayer. Twenty minutes later, when she returned, the ring had disappeared.

Soon everyone was searching under the carpets and behind the cushions, but the ring was nowhere to be found. Aunt Huda crossed her arms and looked towards the kitchen. "Maryam only started working here last month," she said quietly. "Nobody else was near that bathroom." Maryam's face went pale, and Lina noticed that her hands were shaking. "We shouldn't jump to conclusions," Lina said firmly. "A good detective needs evidence first."

Lina went straight to the bathroom and examined the scene carefully. The window had been left wide open, and the sill was covered in a thin layer of dust from the garden. There were no fingerprints in the dust, only some tiny scratches, as if something small had walked across it. Next to the scratches lay a single brown feather. Lina photographed everything and wrote down the details in her notebook.

Next, Lina interviewed her mother, who had been cooking lunch. "Maryam was with me in the kitchen the whole time," her mother said. "She was cutting vegetables, and she never left the room." That gave Maryam an alibi, but it didn't explain where the ring had gone. Lina chewed her pencil and frowned. Someone, or something, had taken it.

Then her little brother Saud came running in with a complaint of his own. "Somebody stole my silver key ring last week!" he said. "I left it on the balcony, and it just vanished." Grandfather laughed and said, "Things have been going missing all month, and those noisy birds in the palm tree have been driving me crazy." Suddenly, Lina's eyes lit up, because she remembered reading that some birds love to collect shiny objects.

To test her theory, Lina set a trap. She folded a piece of shiny silver paper, placed it on the windowsill and hid behind the curtain with her phone ready. For a long time, nothing happened, and her legs began to ache. Then a brown bird with a bright yellow beak landed on the sill, picked up the paper and flew off towards the tall palm tree. "Got you!" Lina whispered, and she had recorded the whole thing.

Uncle Khalid fetched a ladder and climbed carefully up the palm tree while everyone watched from below. "There are no eggs, so I won't disturb any chicks," he called down. A moment later, he gave a loud shout of surprise. Inside the untidy nest were Saud's key ring, two bottle caps, the silver paper and, shining in the middle of it all, Grandmother's gold ring.

Aunt Huda turned to Maryam and said, "I'm truly sorry, I judged you without any reason." Maryam smiled and accepted her apology, and Grandmother hugged Lina tightly. "From now on, you are the official detective of this family," she announced, and everyone laughed. That evening, Lina opened her notebook and wrote two final lines: "Case closed. Look for the truth, not for someone to blame."

Why did Lina believe Maryam was innocent?
options: Maryam showed Lina her empty pockets

options: To move quickly from room to room

options: The tiny scratches and the feather on the windowsill

options: Birds are dangerous and should be removed

pages.text: Faisal had read every superhero comic in his school library, so he knew exactly what a superpower should look like. When his own power finally arrived, on an ordinary Tuesday in Jeddah, it was nothing like the comics. He knocked a glass of mango juice off the kitchen table, and suddenly the whole world stopped. The glass hung in the air, the clock on the wall went silent, and his mother froze in the middle of a sentence.

Over the next week, Faisal tested his power as carefully as a scientist. He discovered three rules. He could stop time only once a day, it lasted exactly three seconds, and while everything else was frozen, he could only move as slowly as he normally did. Three seconds wasn't even long enough to catch the glass of juice, which had landed on his foot.

"So you can't fly, you can't lift cars, and you can't run fast," his best friend Omar said, trying not to laugh. "Your superpower is basically a very long blink." Faisal had told nobody else, and now he was beginning to wish he hadn't told Omar either. He had tried to use his power to score a goal in football, but by the time he had taken two steps, time had started again and the goalkeeper had caught the ball. "Real heroes have real powers," he said sadly.

That weekend, Faisal helped his grandfather in his small spice shop in Al-Balad, the old part of the city. The narrow street sloped down towards the main road, and men pushed heavy carts full of boxes up and down it all day. His grandfather noticed that Faisal looked unhappy. "In my experience," the old man said, weighing a bag of cardamom, "the people who make a difference aren't always the strongest ones. They're the ones who pay attention." Faisal nodded politely, but he didn't really understand.

In the afternoon, his little cousin Yousef came to visit and immediately ran outside to chase a cat. At the top of the street, a delivery man had left his cart for a moment, and it was loaded with wooden boxes of dates. Without warning, the cart began to roll. It picked up speed as it rattled down the hill, heading straight for Yousef, who hadn't noticed anything.

Faisal stopped time without even thinking about it. Everything went silent, and he knew he had only three seconds, so he couldn't possibly reach Yousef or push the heavy cart away. Instead of panicking, he did what his grandfather had said: he paid attention. He noticed a thick rope hanging from the cart, and he saw that its end was lying right next to an iron ring on the wall of the shop. With his last second, he stepped forward and dropped the rope through the ring.

Time started again with a crash of noise. The rope pulled tight, the cart jerked to a stop just a metre from Yousef, and two boxes fell off and broke open, spilling dates all over the street. Yousef stared at the cart, then at the cat, then burst into tears. The delivery man ran down the hill, apologising again and again, and people came out of their shops to see what had happened. Nobody could explain how the rope had got through the ring.

Later, while they were picking up dates together, his grandfather looked at Faisal with a curious smile. "Quick thinking," was all he said, but Faisal had a feeling the old man understood more than he showed. That night, Faisal began drawing his own comic, about a hero called Captain Three Seconds. On the first page, Omar asked the captain what anyone could possibly do with just three seconds, and Faisal wrote the answer in big letters: "Enough, if you use them wisely."

options: Time started again before he could reach the ball

How did Faisal stop the cart?
options: He pushed it away with his hands
He carried Yousef out of the way
He put the cart's rope through an iron ring on the wall

questions.q: What can we guess about Faisal's grandfather at the end?
options: He may suspect that Faisal did something special
He is angry about the broken boxes
He did not see anything that happened

pages.text: Every winter, Faisal's family drove into the desert north of Hail for three days of camping. This year, thirteen-year-old Faisal had brought a power bank, two games and a new map app on his phone. "Who needs the stars when you have satellites?" he joked, while his grandfather put up the tent. Grandpa Saleh only smiled and poured the cardamom coffee.

That first night, Grandpa pointed at the sky above the dunes. "That small, steady star is Al-Jadi, and it always sits in the north," he said. "Our grandfathers crossed this desert by following it." Faisal nodded politely, but he was secretly checking his phone. His sister Lama, who was eleven, listened to every word.

The next afternoon, their father asked them to collect dry wood for the fire and warned them to come back before sunset. Faisal promised, sure that his app would guide them home. They walked from dune to dune, picking up branches and following the tracks of a desert fox, and they didn't notice how far they had gone.

When the sun disappeared, the sand turned grey and every dune looked the same. Faisal took out his phone, but the screen flashed once and went black. "The battery's dead, and I left the power bank in the car," he whispered. Lama grabbed his arm. "We're lost in the middle of nowhere!"

For a moment, Faisal felt panic rising in his chest. Then he remembered Grandpa's calm voice. "Keep calm," he told Lama, and himself. "We walked north all afternoon, so now we need to go south." They looked up at the sky, which was slowly filling with thousands of stars.

"There it is," Lama said, pointing. "Small and steady, just like Grandpa said." Faisal turned so that Al-Jadi was behind him, and they began walking with the star at their backs, even though the wind was cold and the branches felt heavier with every step.

After nearly an hour, Faisal noticed a faint orange light far ahead. Then a smell reached them on the wind: wood smoke and cardamom. "That's our fire!" Lama shouted, and they ran the last part, sliding down the soft sand. Their father was already hurrying towards them with a torch, looking worried and relieved at the same time.

Later, wrapped in blankets beside the fire, Faisal handed Grandpa the wood they had carried all that way. "I owe you an apology," he said. "Satellites are useful, but the stars never run out of battery." Grandpa laughed and poured him a cup of coffee. "Tomorrow night," he said, "I'll teach you three more."

options: The battery died and the power bank was in the car.

stories.title: The Box in the Library Wall

pages.text: Omar had a secret that nobody in Class 2B knew about: his hands shook whenever he had to speak in front of people. So when Mr. Saleh announced that every student would present the morning school radio this term, Omar's heart sank. "You're next Sunday, Omar," the teacher said with a smile. Omar nodded, but inside he was already searching for an excuse.

That afternoon, builders were knocking down an old wall in the library to make space for new computers. Omar and his best friend Hamad stayed behind to help carry books, and that was when Omar noticed something shining in the dust. It was a small metal box, covered in rust, with a date scratched on the lid: 1999. "Treasure!" Hamad whispered, his eyes wide.

Instead of gold, the box held a folded letter, a cassette tape and a faded photo of a boy holding a football trophy. The letter began: "To the student who finds this, I hope you are braver than me." The writer explained that he had run away from the school radio three times because he was too scared to speak. He ended with a challenge: "If you are scared too, do it anyway, and do it for both of us." It was signed with only two letters: K.M.

Omar read the letter again and again that night, as if the boy had written it just for him. "We have to find out who K.M. is," he told Hamad the next morning. They searched through old school yearbooks in the library, but the pages from 1999 were missing, perhaps lost when the library had been moved. They asked the older teachers too, but nobody remembered a boy who was afraid of the microphone.

Then Hamad had an idea. "The cassette! Maybe there's a voice on it." His grandfather still had an old cassette player, so the boys listened to the tape after Asr prayer, holding their breath. A boy's nervous voice said, "Good morning, school..." and then stopped, followed by silence and laughter in the background. Omar felt his cheeks burn, because he knew exactly how that boy had felt.

On Saturday, the headmaster, Mr. Khalid Al-Mansour, gave a speech in the hall about the new library. His voice was calm, strong and confident, and everyone listened in silence. Then Omar noticed a photo on the wall behind him: the school football team of 1999. In the front row, holding the same trophy, was the boy from the box.

After the speech, Omar knocked nervously on the headmaster's door and placed the letter on his desk. Mr. Khalid read it slowly, then laughed softly and shook his head. "I had completely forgotten about this," he admitted. "I was so shy that my knees shook like leaves, but one day I decided that fear would not make my choices for me." He looked at Omar carefully and asked, "Are you presenting the radio soon?"

On Sunday morning, Omar stood in front of the whole school with the microphone in his hand, and his hands were shaking just as they always did. He took a deep breath, looked at Hamad in the front row, and then saw Mr. Khalid at the back, giving him a small nod. "Good morning, school," Omar began, and this time the silence that followed was the silence of people listening. He read the old letter aloud, and when he finished, the applause was louder than he had ever imagined. He had done it, for both of them.

options: To tell Omar to stop speaking
To encourage Omar and show he believed in him
To show that Omar had made a mistake

pages.text: Every evening after Maghrib prayer, Yousef sat with his grandfather on the balcony of their flat in Jeddah. Jiddo Saleh had been a sailor when he was young, and his stories were full of storms, pearls and faraway ports. Recently, though, he had started to forget things, like where he had put his glasses or what day it was. So Yousef had decided to record his stories on his phone before they disappeared like footprints in the sand.

"Tell me about the green door again," Yousef said one evening, pressing the red button. Jiddo smiled. "When I was a boy, I lived in Al-Balad, in a house with a green wooden door. Every morning I bought bread from the baker on the corner, then ran down to the sea, counting the steps: two hundred and twelve." Yousef laughed, because Jiddo always remembered that number, even on days when he forgot his own phone number.

The next Friday, the whole family went to Al-Balad to visit the old market. Mum was busy choosing spices, Reem wanted to look at the pottery, and Yousef was supposed to keep an eye on Jiddo. But for a moment, he was distracted by a man selling old coins. When he turned around, his grandfather had vanished into the crowd.

Yousef's heart sank. "Mum! Jiddo's gone!" he shouted. Mum went pale and immediately called Dad, who was still parking the car, while little Reem began to cry. The narrow streets were packed with people, and from behind, every old man in a white thobe looked exactly like Jiddo.

Dad arrived, out of breath, and the family split up to search. Yousef ran up and down the alleys, asking shopkeepers if they had seen an old man with a wooden walking stick. Nobody had. Then, standing in the shade to catch his breath, he took out his phone and listened again to Tuesday's recording: the green door, the bakery on the corner, two hundred and twelve steps.

"He hasn't got lost," Yousef said slowly. "He's gone home." He hurried to an elderly shopkeeper and asked whether he knew an old house with a green door near a bakery. The man thought for a moment, then pointed down a quiet lane. "The bakery closed years ago, but the green door is still there."

Yousef found him sitting on the stone step of a tall old house, its green paint cracked and faded. Jiddo was resting his walking stick across his knees and gazing up at the carved wooden window. "Yousef," he said calmly, as if nothing unusual had happened, "I wanted to see if it was still here." Yousef sat down beside him, so relieved that he couldn't speak, and quickly sent a message to his parents.

That evening, the family drank cardamom coffee and ate dates together on the balcony, and Mum held Jiddo's hand a little longer than usual. "From now on, we'll go to Al-Balad together every month," Dad promised, "and you can show us all your places." Jiddo nodded, then looked at Yousef with a twinkle in his eye. "Press the red button," he said. "There are still many stories you haven't heard." Yousef smiled and pressed it, because now he understood that some stories aren't only for remembering; they can also lead you home.

options: She was still cold from being outside

pages.text: Every summer, Yusuf visited his grandfather's farm in the mountains near Abha, where coffee trees grew on narrow stone terraces. This year, he arrived with a backpack full of wires, a small solar panel and his father's old phone. "What is all that?" asked Grandpa Saleh, raising an eyebrow. "It's my project for the school science competition," Yusuf explained proudly.

Yusuf had been reading about flash floods, which can fill a dry valley with water in just a few minutes. Below the farm was a wadi where shepherds often rested and families sometimes stopped for picnics. His plan was to put a water sensor higher up the valley and connect it to the old phone, so it would send a warning if the water level rose suddenly. Grandpa smiled kindly. "For seventy years I have watched the sky, my boy, and it tells me everything I need to know."

Still, Grandpa helped him carry the equipment up a rocky path to a narrow part of the valley, two kilometres above the farm. They fixed the sensor to a large rock and placed the solar panel where it would catch the morning sun. When Yusuf tested it by pouring a bottle of water over the sensor, his own phone beeped a second later: "WARNING: Water rising!" His cousin Huda, who had come to watch, clapped her hands. "Not bad for someone who can't even fix his own bike," she teased.

For a whole week, nothing happened at all. The sky stayed clear and blue, and the phone stayed silent. Yusuf began to worry that his project would seem boring to the judges because it had no exciting results. Then one afternoon, Grandpa looked towards the mountains and frowned. "Clouds are building in the north," he said, "but they're far away, so it won't rain here today."

That evening, while the family was having dinner on the roof, Yusuf's phone suddenly beeped loudly. He looked at the screen, and his heart began to race. The water in the upper valley had risen thirty centimetres in only two minutes, yet above the farm there wasn't a single drop of rain. "The storm must be falling higher up the mountain," Yusuf said, jumping to his feet. "And all that water is coming down here!"

From the roof, they could see the lights of a car parked in the wadi below, where a family had stopped for a picnic. Grandpa didn't waste a second. He grabbed his torch and hurried down the path, with Yusuf and Huda right behind him, shouting and waving their arms. The father of the family looked confused at first, but as soon as Grandpa explained, he helped his wife and children into the car and drove up onto the road.

Less than ten minutes later, they heard a deep roar, like a train coming through the mountains. A wall of brown water rushed through the valley, carrying stones and branches over the exact place where the car had been parked. The family's little girl held her mother's hand tightly and stared. "If you hadn't come," her father said quietly to Yusuf, "I don't want to imagine what might have happened."

A month later, Yusuf won second place at the competition, but that wasn't the best news. The local council was so impressed that they decided to put sensors like his in other valleys across the region. On the day the first new sensor was installed, Grandpa Saleh asked Yusuf to show him how to read the warning messages on his phone. "The sky tells me a lot," he said with a smile, "but I've learned that it doesn't tell me everything. From now on, I'll keep one eye on the clouds and the other on this screen."

options: He refused to leave the wadi
He put his family in the car and drove up onto the road

options: He believed technology and his experience could work together

stories.title: The Man Who Caught the Light

pages.text: Cairo, 1015. Every morning, twelve-year-old Yusuf carried bread and dates to a quiet house near the great mosque of Al-Azhar. People in the market whispered that the man inside had lost his mind. "Don't look into his eyes," the baker warned. "They say he talks to the walls." Yusuf was nervous, but his family needed the coins that the job paid.

The man was called Al-Hasan Ibn al-Haytham, and he had once been a famous scholar from Basra. Years earlier, the ruler of Egypt had ordered him to stop the flooding of the River Nile. When Ibn al-Haytham travelled south and studied the river, he realised that the task was impossible. Afraid of the ruler's anger, he had decided to act as if he were mad, so he was locked in his house instead of being punished.

One hot afternoon, Yusuf found the door open and the house completely dark. "Come in quickly and close the door behind you," a calm voice said. In the blackness, Yusuf noticed a tiny hole in the wooden shutter, no bigger than a grain of rice. On the opposite wall, there was a picture of the street outside, glowing in full colour, but it was upside down!

Yusuf gasped and nearly dropped his basket. "Is this magic?" he asked. "Not at all," Ibn al-Haytham laughed, sounding perfectly sane. "Light travels in straight lines, so the rays from the top of that camel cross through the hole and land at the bottom of the wall." For the first time, Yusuf realised that the 'madman' was the cleverest person he had ever met.

From then on, Yusuf stayed longer every day to help. He held candles at different distances, measured shadows and recorded the results, while the scholar wrote quickly on his papers. "The ancient Greek thinkers believed that our eyes send out light," Ibn al-Haytham explained. "But I never accept an idea just because a famous person said it. We must test it ourselves."

One evening, a guard knocked loudly at the door, and Yusuf's heart was in his mouth. If the ruler discovered the truth, his master could be punished severely. Thinking fast, Yusuf grabbed a cooking pot and began banging it like a drum, while Ibn al-Haytham sang nonsense songs at the top of his voice. The guard shook his head, muttered something about "that poor crazy man", and walked away.

Years passed, and in 1021 news arrived that the ruler had died. At last, Ibn al-Haytham was free to walk in the sunlight again. By then, he had filled seven books with his discoveries about light, mirrors and the human eye. "These pages would not exist without you, my friend," he told Yusuf, who was now a young man.

Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics was later translated and studied by scientists around the world for hundreds of years. Today, many people call him the father of the scientific method, and every camera works on the idea he tested in that dark room. Yusuf grew up to become a teacher himself. Whenever a student asked him what makes a true hero, he would smile, cover the window and leave just one small hole for the light.

options: He could not do the ruler's task and was afraid of his anger.
He wanted people in the market to leave him alone.
He was tired of travelling and wanted to stay at home.

options: A painting of the River Nile
An upside-down picture of the street outside
A shadow of Ibn al-Haytham's hand

questions.q: In the story, the word "sane" means:
Why did Yusuf start banging the cooking pot when the guard came?
options: He wanted to call for help from the neighbours.
He wanted the guard to believe his master was still mad.
He was practising music for a celebration.

questions.q: What does Yusuf's action at the end of the story suggest about a true hero?
options: A true hero is curious and tests ideas to find the truth.
A true hero must be rich and famous.
A true hero always obeys every order without question.

stories.title: The River That Came From Nowhere

pages.text: Noura had always been the weather expert in her family. While her cousins checked football scores, she checked wind speeds and cloud maps on her phone. So when her grandfather invited everyone to his farm near the mountains for the weekend, she was the first to look at the forecast. "Clear skies all day," she announced. "Perfect for a picnic in the wadi."

The wadi was a wide, dry valley behind the farm, full of smooth stones and soft sand. Her younger brother Saad and their cousins Hamad and Lulwa raced ahead, laughing and kicking up dust. Grandfather walked slowly behind them with his stick, while Mother and Aunt Huda spread a carpet under an acacia tree. Above them, the sky was a perfect, burning blue.

After lunch, Noura noticed something strange. Far away, over the mountains, dark clouds had gathered, tall and grey like towers. A low rumble of thunder rolled across the valley, so quiet that nobody else seemed to hear it. She opened her weather app again, and this time a yellow warning was flashing: heavy rain in the highlands.

"Grandfather, it's raining in the mountains," she said. He was already looking at the horizon, and his face had become serious. "When I was a boy, we had a saying," he replied. "The wadi remembers every drop that falls on the mountains, and sooner or later it brings them home." Noura felt a cold shiver, even though the air was hot.

She understood immediately. All that rain would run down the slopes and into the valley, straight towards them. "Everyone, we need to move to higher ground now!" she shouted. Hamad rolled his eyes. "You're worrying about nothing. There isn't a single cloud above us!"

Then Lulwa pointed at the ground. A thin line of brown water was sliding between the stones, quietly, like a snake. A strange smell of wet earth filled the air, and a deep roar was growing louder somewhere up the valley. Nobody argued after that.

They grabbed the carpet and the baskets and hurried up the rocky bank, with Saad holding Grandfather's arm. They had only just reached the top when the flood arrived. A wall of muddy water rushed through the wadi, carrying branches, stones and even their forgotten football. The acacia tree where they had been sitting minutes before was now standing in a fast, wild river.

For a long time, nobody spoke, and then Hamad turned to Noura. "I should have listened to you," he said quietly. Grandfather put his hand on her shoulder and smiled. "Your phone and my old saying told the same story," he said, "and a wise person listens to both." The next morning, the wadi was dry again, but Noura knew she would never trust a blue sky so easily.

options: They saw water and heard a roar coming

pages.text: Every afternoon, Faisal walked home through the narrow streets of Al-Balad, the old part of Jeddah. He always stopped under the same tall house, with its coral-stone walls and dark wooden windows called rawasheen. One window had a hole where a carved panel had once been, like a missing tooth in a smile. "Your great-grandfather made that window," his grandfather had told him, "but the last piece was broken long before you were born."

At school, Mr. Khalid announced a competition: the winning student would design a large mural for the entrance of the new community centre. "Show us something that belongs to this city," he said. Faisal's best friend, Omar, was already sketching camels and palm trees, but Faisal just stared at his empty page. He had never been good at drawing, and his camels looked like potatoes with legs.

That evening, Faisal sat with his grandfather on the roof and admitted that he had no ideas at all. Grandfather went inside and came back with an old notebook. Inside there were no pictures, only circles, lines and stars, all made with a compass and a ruler. "Every pattern begins with one circle," he said. "If you understand the circle, you can build anything."

For two weeks, Faisal filled page after page with eight-pointed stars that joined together like a chain. His final design was a huge wall of stars inspired by the old window, with one shape in the centre left empty. The night before the deadline, he left it on the kitchen table. In the morning, he found his little brother Saud beside it, holding an empty cup of karak tea, and the paper had soaked up every drop.

"I'm sorry! I was only looking at it," Saud cried. Faisal wanted to shout, but when he saw the tears in his brother's eyes, he took a deep breath instead. There were only three hours left before he had to hand in his design. "Then you can help me," he said, grabbing a new sheet, his compass and his ruler. "Hold the paper flat and don't let it move."

At first his hands were shaking, and his first circle came out wrong. Then he remembered Grandfather's words and started again, slowly. Circle by circle, line by line, the stars returned, as if they had been waiting inside his head all along. This time he noticed something he had missed before: the empty shape in the centre was exactly the size of the missing panel in the old window. He finished in the nick of time and ran to school with ink all over his fingers.

A week later, Mr. Khalid read out the winner's name, and Faisal was so surprised that Omar had to push him out of his chair. "The judges loved the way your design connects the past and the present," Mr. Khalid said. "But they want to know why there's an empty space in the middle." Faisal smiled. "Because some pieces of our city are still missing," he replied, "and someone has to finish them."

That spring, the whole class helped to paint the mural, but the best moment came afterwards. With the owner's permission, Faisal and his grandfather carved a small wooden panel in the same star pattern and fitted it into the old window in Al-Balad. Saud insisted on holding the screws, and nobody argued. Under the evening sun, the window looked complete for the first time in fifty years, like a smile with no missing teeth.

What ruined Faisal's first design?
In the story, what does "in the nick of time" mean?
options: Just before it was too late

questions.q: Why did Faisal ask Saud to help him instead of shouting at him?
options: He wanted Saud to draw the stars
He saw Saud was truly sorry and chose to forgive him
He was too tired to be angry

questions.q: What is the main message of the empty space in Faisal's design?
options: He did not have enough time to finish it

pages.text: Every summer, Noura spent a week at her grandmother's old house in Al-Balad, the historic heart of Jeddah. The house had tall wooden windows, narrow stairs and a cool room full of things that nobody used any more. On a high shelf in that room stood an hourglass made of dark wood and glass. "Look at it as much as you like," her grandmother always said, "but never turn it over."

One hot afternoon, while her grandmother was resting, Noura climbed onto a chair to take a closer look. The sand inside wasn't yellow but silver, and it seemed to shine on its own. She told herself that she would only hold it for a moment, but as she lifted it, it slipped in her hands and turned upside down. The room began to spin, and the silver sand started to fall.

When Noura opened her eyes, she was standing in the same street, but everything had changed. The parked cars and air conditioners had disappeared, and the street was crowded with carts, donkeys and men selling dates and fabric. An old song was playing on a radio in a shop, and a calendar on the wall said 1965. With her heart beating fast, Noura realised that she had travelled back almost sixty years.

Near an old well, a girl of about her age was searching the ground, close to tears. "My father trusted me with the key to his shop, and I've lost it," she explained. "If I don't find it before sunset, he won't be able to lock the door tonight." Noura could feel the hourglass in her pocket and guessed she didn't have long, but she couldn't just walk away. "Don't worry," she said with a smile. "Two pairs of eyes are better than one."

Together they retraced the girl's steps through the market, checking under baskets and between the stones. "Did you stop anywhere on the way?" Noura asked, and the girl remembered that she had bent down to drink from a water jar outside the mosque. Sure enough, a small brass key was lying in the shadow beside it. The girl, whose name was Hessa, laughed with relief and hugged her new friend.

Then Hessa noticed the phone in Noura's hand. "What is that strange glass box?" she asked, her eyes wide with wonder. Noura showed her a photo of modern Jeddah, with its towers shining by the sea, but before she could explain, she saw that only a few grains of sand were left. Feeling dizzy, she put the phone down on the edge of the well to hold the hourglass with both hands, and the whole world disappeared.

Noura woke up on the floor of the cool room, with the hourglass lying beside her. Her heart sank when she checked her pocket, because her phone was gone. She hurried downstairs, ready to apologise, but her grandmother was already waiting for her with a small tin box and a gentle smile. "I've been keeping this for you for a very long time," she said.

Inside the box was Noura's phone, old and dusty, its battery long dead. Next to it lay a piece of paper, yellow with age, covered in a child's careful handwriting: "For the girl who helped me find my father's key. I promise to keep your glass box safe until you come back." At the bottom was a name, Hessa, and Noura looked up at her grandmother in amazement. "Some things only happen at the right time," her grandmother said softly, "and today, at last, was the right time."

questions.q: What was special about the sand in the hourglass?
options: It was silver and seemed to shine on its own.
It was yellow and very old.
It moved upwards instead of down.

questions.q: Where did Noura and Hessa find the lost key?
options: Under a basket in the market
Beside a water jar outside the mosque
At the bottom of the old well

questions.q: In the story, the word 'relief' is closest in meaning to...
options: a feeling that a worry has gone

questions.q: Why did Noura leave her phone in 1965?
options: She gave it to Hessa as a present.
Someone took it from her in the market.
She put it down to hold the hourglass with both hands.

questions.q: What can we understand from the ending of the story?
options: Hessa, the girl from 1965, was Noura's grandmother.
Noura's grandmother found the phone in the street that morning.
Hessa was a friend of Noura's from school.

pages.text: Every morning before school, Reem and her younger brother Faisal walked along the muddy shore near their grandfather's house in Jazan. For two weeks, they had been looking after forty tiny mangrove seedlings, which their science class had planted in the shallow water. Their teacher, Ms. Hanan, had explained that mangrove forests protect the coast from storms and give young fish a safe place to grow. Reem was determined to keep every single plant alive.

But on Thursday morning, Faisal stopped suddenly and pointed. "Reem, look! Six of them are gone!" Where the seedlings had stood the day before, there were only small holes in the mud. Reem felt her heart sink. "Someone is stealing them," she said, "and we're going to get to the bottom of this."

That evening, they told their grandfather, who had been a fisherman for forty years. He listened carefully while he drank his tea. "Before you accuse anyone, you need evidence," he said. "Watch the shore at low tide, when the water goes out. The sea always tells its secrets then." Faisal suddenly had an idea: they could hide his old phone in a tree and record a video.

The next afternoon, they fixed the phone to a low branch and pointed it at the seedlings. After school the following day, they checked the video, full of excitement. For a long time, nothing happened except the tide slowly going out. Then, just after sunset, something moved across the mud. Faisal leaned closer to the screen. "It's not a person at all," he whispered.

Dozens of small red crabs were climbing out of holes in the mud. With their claws, they grabbed the soft young leaves and pulled the seedlings down into their burrows. Reem couldn't help laughing, even though she was disappointed. "So our thieves have eight legs!" Grandfather smiled. "Crabs are part of the mangrove forest too," he said. "Big trees can survive them, but baby plants need protection."

But how could they protect the seedlings? Then Reem remembered the pile of plastic bottles she had collected during a beach clean-up the month before. "What if we cut the bottles and put one around each seedling, like a wall?" she asked. "Rubbish that saves a forest? That's genius!" Faisal said. All weekend, they washed and cut the bottles, then pushed them into the mud, leaving the tops open for sunlight and air.

A week later, they checked the shore again, and they were over the moon. Every protected seedling was still standing, and some even had new green leaves. When Ms. Hanan came to see, she was so impressed that she asked them to present their idea to the whole school. Soon, students were bringing bottles from home, and the project grew from forty plants to more than three hundred.

Months later, when the young trees were strong enough, the bottles were removed and recycled, so no plastic was left on the shore. One evening, Reem and Faisal sat with their grandfather and watched the sun set over their small green forest. Tiny fish were swimming between the roots. "You solved the mystery," Grandfather said, "but you also made peace with the crabs." Reem smiled, because she had learned that protecting nature doesn't mean fighting it, but understanding it.

stories.title: The Birds on the Bakery Shelf

pages.text: Every morning before school, Omar helped his grandfather at the small bakery in the old part of Taif. He loved the smell of fresh bread and the heavy sound of the oven door closing. But recently, something strange had been happening. Each morning, one loaf disappeared from the shelf by the back door, and in its place there was a tiny wooden bird.

"Someone is stealing from us, Jiddo," Omar said, holding up the seventh bird. His grandfather simply smiled and put it on the high shelf next to the others. "Stealing? A thief doesn't leave presents," he replied. Omar wasn't convinced, so he decided to find out the truth himself.

The next morning, he arrived an hour early and hid behind the flour sacks. Just as the sky was turning pink, the back door opened quietly. A thin boy about his own age stepped inside, took a loaf, and carefully placed a small carved falcon on the shelf. Omar jumped out. "Caught you red-handed!" he shouted.

The boy froze, and the bread almost fell from his hands. "I'm not a thief," he said in a shaking voice. "My name is Sami. We moved here three months ago, and my father hasn't been able to work since his accident." He looked down at the floor. "I can't pay with money, so I pay with what I make."

Before Omar could answer, his grandfather appeared in the doorway. "Good morning, Sami," he said warmly, as if he had been expecting him. Omar stared at him. "You knew all along?" His grandfather nodded and explained that he had left that loaf by the back door on purpose every single day.

Later, while Sami ate breakfast with them, Grandfather told a story Omar had never heard before. "When I was a boy, my family had very little," he said. "A baker in Makkah gave us bread every morning, and he never once made me feel ashamed. Real kindness doesn't only fill someone's stomach, Omar. It also protects their pride."

Omar felt his face go hot as he remembered shouting at Sami. "I'm sorry," he said. "I should have asked before I accused you." Then he looked up at the shelf of wooden birds, and an idea came to him. "Sami, these are amazing. People would buy them, I'm sure of it."

By the end of the month, the shelf above the counter had become the most popular corner of the bakery. Customers came for bread but left with falcons, doves and hoopoes, and Sami's family no longer had to worry about the rent. Every morning, Omar still put one loaf by the back door, just in case someone else needed it. And next to it, he left a small note: "Take what you need. No questions asked."
